blocks.text: Among the species of eagles there is one, unknown to us from other sources, which the Arabs call زمج [zmj] zummag, and barbarous writers zumach and zimiech. Damir, in the chapter On العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] Alokab, or the Eagle: وهو نوعان عقاب وزمج [wa-huwa nawʿān ʿuqāb wa-zummaj] Of it there are two species, okab and zummag. Tardivus in Gesner, p. 170: There are two kinds of eagle: the eagle simply so called; and another, called zimiech or zumach. And again: Whiteness on the head or back of an eagle is a sign of the better eagle, which is called ZUMMACH in Arabic, NAPAM in Syriac, Philadelphe in Greek, MILION in Latin. On these words Gesner remarks: Of these, you will find the Greek and Latin name of the eagle in no reliable author. Yet philadelphe is plainly distorted from the Greek φιλάδελφος [philadelphos]. That this bird was called by this name by the later Greeks, although I have not read it elsewhere, seems to me probable for this reason: no more fitting name could have been given to it, nor one that expresses its nature more vividly. For it is characteristic of the eagle kind to love solitude and to be entirely intolerant of all company. Hence, as soon as the eaglets are able to fly, the mothers ἐκ τῆς νεοττίας αὐτοὺς ἐκβάλλουσι, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου τοῦ περὶ αὐτὴν παντὸς ἀπελαύνουσιν· ἐπέχει γὰρ ἓν ζεῦγος αἰετῶν πολὺν τόπον. διόπερ οὐκ ἐᾷ πλησίον αὑτῶν ἄλλους αὐλισθῆναι [ek tēs neottias autous ekballousi, kai ek tou topou tou peri autēn pantos apelaunousin; epechei gar hen zeugos aietōn polyn topon. dioper ouk ea plēsion hautōn allous aulisthēnai]. So the Philosopher, book 9, chapter 32; and following him Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: The parent also pursues the grown young and drives them far away, as rivals in plunder, of course. And besides, a single pair of eagles needs a large tract to plunder in order to be satisfied. They therefore mark out territories and do not prey close by one another. Aelian, book 2, chapter 39: Κοινωνίαν τε τὴν πρὸς ἄλλον ἥκιστα ἐνδέχεται [Koinōnian te tēn pros allon hēkista endechetai], It admits no fellowship with others. Likewise: Ἀλλήλων ἀπῳκισμένας οἰκοῦσι κα- [col. 336] λιάς, ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ διαφέρεσθαι ὑπὲρ θήρας [Allēlōn apōkismenas oikousi kalias, hyper tou mē diapheresthai hyper thēras]; They nest very far from one another, so that they need not fight over prey. Yet the زمج [zmj] zummag of that kind is truly φιλάδελφος [philadelphos]: it delights in a companion, and does not usually hunt alone, but with a comrade joined to it. Alcamus: الزمج طاير فارسية دو برادران لانه اذا اعجز عن صيده اعانه اخوه [al-zummaj ṭāʾir fārisiyya dū barādarān li-annahu idhā aʿjaza ʿan ṣaydihi aʿānahu akhūhu] Zummag, a bird which in Persian is called DU-BRADRAN (that is, two brothers), because, when its prey escapes it, its brother comes to its aid. Alleiths: الجمز طاير دون العقاب حمرته [III, 98] غالبة تسميه العجم دبران ومن طبعه انه اذا عجز عن صيده اعانه اخوه علي اخذه [al-jmz ṭāʾir dūn al-ʿuqāb ḥumratuhu ghāliba tusammīhi al-ʿajam dbrān wa-min ṭabʿihi annahu idhā ʿajaza ʿan ṣaydihi aʿānahu akhūhu ʿalā akhdhihi] Giummaz (another copy reads better الزمج [al-zummaj] zummag) is a bird below the eagle (that is, like the eagle but smaller), in which redness predominates. It is called in Agem (that is, in Persia) DABRAN (or rather, as before, دو برادران [dū barādarān] DU-BRADRAN, that is, two brothers): it is of its nature that, when it cannot overtake its prey, its brother helps it to catch it. More recent writers say the same of falcons. Vincent, in the Doctrinale, book 16, chapter 156: In catching a heron two falcons are released together: one of them seeks the heights; the other flies low near the ground; so that the one may bring down the flying heron by its onset, and the other may take it when brought down. Of the same bird zummag, Sariph in Abenbitar: هو طاير معروف يصيد به الملوك للطير [huwa ṭāʾir maʿrūf yaṣīdu bihi al-mulūk lil-ṭayr] A well-known bird which kings use in fowling. And Giulbaki: الزمج جنس من الطير يصاد به [al-zummaj jins min al-ṭayr yuṣād bihi] Zummag, a kind of fowling bird. Abuchatim the Andalusian, or Spaniard, also said: انه ذكر العقاب والجمع الزماميج [annahu dhakar al-ʿuqāb wa-al-jamʿ al-zamāmīj] that it is the male of the eagle, whose plural is zemamigio. And Alkazuinius: زمج طاير يقال له بالفارسية رهل [zummaj ṭāʾir yuqālu lahu bil-fārisiyya rhl] Zummag, a bird called in Persian RAHAL. This is another name of this bird in Persia, different from the former du-bradran. And Damir: اهل البزدرة يعدونه من خغاف الجوارح وذلك معروف في عينه وحركته وشدة وثبه والمحمود منه ما كان لونه احمر وهو احد نوعي العقاب ويوصف بالغدر وقلة الالف لكثافة طبعه وقد يقبل التعليم ولكن بعد بطو ومن عادته ان يصيد علي وجه [col. 337] الارض [ahl al-bzdra yaʿuddūnahu min khghāf al-jawāriḥ wa-dhālika maʿrūf fī ʿaynihi wa-ḥarakatihi wa-shiddat wathbihi wa-al-maḥmūd minhu mā kāna lawnuhu aḥmar wa-huwa aḥad nawʿay al-ʿuqāb wa-yūṣafu bil-ghadr wa-qillat al-ilf li-kathāfat ṭabʿihi wa-qad yaqbalu al-taʿlīm wa-lākin baʿda buṭūʾ wa-min ʿādatihi an yaṣīda ʿalā wajh al-arḍ] The people of Albizdara (which is an Arab tribe) count it among those birds which are swiftest in seizing prey. This is shown by its eye and its movement, and the onset with which it rushes on its prey. Among them the one that is reddest is preferred. It is one of the two species of eagle. It is described as treacherous, but slow to learn, because it is stupid by nature. Yet after some delay it at last becomes capable of training. It mostly hunts birds near the surface of the ground. Of the same name, but of a different kind, is the bird زمج الما [zummaj al-mā] zummag of the water, which we have shown in its place ^{a)} to be the catarractes. For the Zummag, a kind of eagle, and the zummag of the water, or [III, 99] catarrhactes, rush upon their prey with equal impetus. Thus eagles are said καταῤῥάσσειν [katarrhassein], that is, to hurl themselves with force upon their prey, as well as the catarrhactes birds, which got their name from this. Hence Eustathius on Iliad 19: Ἅρπη δὲ, ἢ ὁ ἰκτῖνος, ἢ ζῶον ἄλλο ἀετῶδες, ὃ εἰς ὕψος ἀρθὲν εὐχερῶς ὅπη θέλει καταῤῥάσσει [Harpē de, ē ho iktinos, ē zōon allo aetōdes, ho eis hypsos arthen eucherōs hopē thelei katarrhassei]; Harpe is either the kite, or another bird of the eagle kind, which, having risen on high, easily swoops with force wherever it wishes. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: The haliaeetus, poising itself on high, and on seeing a fish in the sea, rushing headlong upon it, that is, καταῤῥάσσων [katarrhassōn]. In the books of the physicians there is much about remedies from this bird. An eye-salve from its gall cures dimness of sight. Its dung, smeared on, removes blotches and freckles. The dung of a man who eats its flesh is useful for palpitations of the heart. These things are to be found in Damir, Abenbitar and Alkazuinius. We have observed that the Greeks of a later age called it Φιλάδελφον [Philadelphon] from its character. The Arabic name زمج [zmj] zummag suggests that it is irascible, since it is formed from anger. For in Arabic زمج zamigia is to be angry, زمج zamag anger, مزمج musinig angry. From this you may infer by a very probable conjecture that the Hebrew אנפה anapha (the species of bird which Moses lists after חסידה hasidah) is the very same as the Arabic زمج [zmj] zummag. For the אנפה anapha too is believed to be an irascible bird, because the Hebrew verb אנף anaph means to be angry, and the contracted noun אף aph means anger or wrath. Thus in Aben Ezra it is said to be so called שיתאנף מהרה, because it is easily angered. And in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, ch. 3, p. 63a, the Hebrews define it as דיה רגזנית, the irascible vulture. For it has been proved above ^{b)} that vultures are often confused with eagles. But, you will say, a reason is added why it is called anapha which agrees little with the nature of the zummag: למה נקרא שמה אנפה שמתאנפת עם חברותיה, Why is it called anapha, a name taken from anger? Because it is angry with its companions. The zummag, on the contrary, is Φιλάδελφος [Philadelphos], and admits its brother, or mate, into partnership in the prey. I answer that it may happen that those who were harmonious and of one mind in the hunt fall out with one another in dividing the prey, and are provoked to anger against each other.
